about.title: About Engawa
about.lead: Engawa (縁側) is a multilingual neighbourhood board for Japan. It connects local information across languages and communities, so everyone can find and share what matters.
about.what_body: In one neighbourhood, information is spread over places that do not reach each other: a paper notice at the entrance in Japanese only, the residents' LINE group, WeChat and KakaoTalk groups in other languages, the city's mail and its loudspeakers. Each reaches its own people, and the people who need it most are often in none of them.
about.why_body: What matters in a neighbourhood, from a water outage next week to a shelter that opened tonight, should reach everyone who lives there. Most of it is written in Japanese only, and many neighbours read another language first.
about.how_body: Anyone drops in what they already have: a photo of a paper notice, a chat screenshot or a few lines of text. It becomes a card in Japanese, English, Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese and easy Japanese (やさしい日本語), with its source and its time. A report about something already on the board joins that card as another source instead of becoming a duplicate.
about.how_ask: Readers ask the board in their own language. The answer uses only the board's cards and links to the ones it comes from, or says that there is no information yet.
about.layer_claude_body: Reads the input, extracts the facts, hides the names and contact details it finds, compares the report with the cards already on the board, proposes whether it is new, the same, an update or a conflict, and translates it. Its job is to organize, and it is told never to add facts.
about.layer_code_body: Every answer from Claude must match a fixed format. A place that is not on the board is dropped, a time that cannot be read is left empty, and a phone number or email address left in the text rejects the result. Code also keeps the order of trust (official, then seen firsthand, then heard from others), so a weaker report cannot replace a stronger one: both are shown. Rumours, and anything about a specific person's health or situation, are held back.
about.layer_people_body: The board admin decides whether what was held is published, hides what should not be on the board, and is the only one who can confirm a card as official. Readers can mark a card “Still true” or “No longer true”.
about.how_limits: None of this makes a card verified. Detection can miss a name, and a card is only as reliable as its sources, which is why every card shows them.
about.who_maria: Maria reads English and not Japanese. The notice about the water distribution is taped to the entrance in Japanese only. On the board Maria reads it in English and asks where to get water.
about.who_sato: 佐藤さん photographs the notice at the shelter entrance. That one photo is what everyone else reads, in six languages, easy Japanese included.
about.who_chen: チェンさん forwards a WeChat screenshot saying the convenience store in front of the station is open and has water. The names in it never reach the board. The information does, in Japanese too.
about.who_groups: And the people who already put up the notices: event organisers, neighbourhood associations (自治会), property managers. One card reaches each resident in their own language. Later, perhaps, municipalities too.
about.everyday_heading: Every day, and in a disaster
about.everyday_body: Most days the board carries ordinary notices: water outages, garbage days, building notices, local events. That is the point: people get to know the board before they need it.
about.everyday_disaster: In a disaster the same board switches to disaster mode, by the board admin, or by itself when an official city message names an emergency such as an evacuation order: a red strip at the top, official and danger cards first, then water, shelters and medical help, all in six languages.
about.numbers_body: At the end of September 2026, {cityTotal} foreign residents lived in Kawasaki City, {wardTotal} of them in Nakahara Ward (Kawasaki City, 管区別年齢別外国人住民人口, Basic Resident Register, end of September 2026). At the end of March 2026 the largest groups in Nakahara Ward were from China ({zh}), Korea ({ko}), Vietnam ({vi}), the Philippines ({ph}) and Nepal ({np}) (Kawasaki City, 外国人国籍地域別統計, end of March 2026). The board's languages follow these numbers; easy Japanese is for the many who read some Japanese but not a notice.
about.trust_1: Every card shows where it came from (an official notice, seen firsthand or heard from others), how many sources back it and when it last changed.
about.trust_2: When sources disagree, both statements are shown side by side. Rumours, and anything about a specific person's health or situation, go to the board admin instead of being published.
about.trust_3: A card past its time turns grey and says “May be outdated”. An official notice stays “unconfirmed” until the board admin, a person, confirms it.
about.data_1: Your exact location never leaves your phone. If you choose to add your area, the browser sends only the name of the district (町丁目), and it is shown as self-reported, never as verified.
about.data_2: Claude replaces the private names, phone numbers, room numbers, chat IDs and number plates it finds with placeholders such as ［名前］, and code rejects any text in which a phone number or email address is left. Detection can still miss something. The original chat screenshot is never shown and is deleted when processing ends; a copy with what Claude found covered appears on the card only if all of it could be covered.
about.data_3: Everything has an expiry. A card is deleted 30 days after the time it was valid for, a photo of a notice with its card, and the browser identifier 90 days after its last use. Questions typed into the ask box are not stored.
about.data_4: There are no accounts, and the board is not indexed by search engines. The full retention table is published with the project's source code (docs/PRIVACY.md).
about.join_1: Drop in what you see: a photo of the paper at your entrance, a screenshot from your group chat, a few lines of text. On every board it starts with “{button}”.
about.join_2: Put the board up where people pass. Every board has a printable poster with a QR code, and any card can be printed as a notice in six languages to hang next to the Japanese original.
about.join_3: Bring Engawa to your neighbourhood. A neighbourhood association, a building manager or a community group that wants a board for its area, or wants to put its notices on one, can get in touch on GitHub. Engawa has no partnership with any city: the city messages on the boards come from services the cities offer to everyone, Kawasaki's and Fukuoka's disaster mail, subscribed to like any resident, and the broadcast text Shibuya publishes on its disaster portal.
about.after_heading: Where it stands, and what is next
about.status_body: Engawa was built in one week for Built with Claude: Japan 2026. Six boards are live: Musashi-Kosugi and Mizonokuchi in Kawasaki, Shibuya and Ueno in Tokyo, Sapporo Odori, and Hakata in Fukuoka.
about.status_working: Working today: drop-in from photos, screenshots, text and the loudspeaker, cards in six languages, merging, asking the board, alerts, offline reading, the poster and the printable notice, and disaster mode. City messages are connected to four boards: Kawasaki's mail to Musashi-Kosugi and Mizonokuchi, Shibuya's broadcast feed to Shibuya, Fukuoka's mail to Hakata. Ueno and Sapporo Odori have none yet.
about.after_body: After the event, Engawa is meant to run in two layers: one platform operator for every board, and a local owner for each board.

inbox.heading: Official inbox
inbox.intro: The city sends the text of each disaster radio broadcast (防災行政無線) by email, for example メールニュースかわさき. A mail forwarder can post those mails here. Each one becomes an official card, and a card made from what a neighbour heard is updated instead of repeated. Setup: docs/INBOX.md in the source code.

home.lead: Engawa connects local information across languages and communities, so everyone can find and share what matters.
home.boards_lead: Explore local information from boards across Japan.
home.step1_body: A photo of a paper notice, a chat screenshot or a few lines of text: whatever you already have.
home.step2_body: Claude reads it, hides the names and contact details it finds, compares it with the cards already on the board and translates it. Each card keeps its source and time.
home.step3_body: Read the cards in your language and ask the board a question. Answers point to the cards they come from.
home.why_1: One neighbour posts on LINE. Another on WeChat or KakaoTalk. The city prints paper and runs the loudspeaker.
home.why_2: The information is out there. It just does not arrive.
home.why_3: An engawa is the veranda of a Japanese house, between inside and outside, where neighbours drop by and talk.
home.disaster_heading: When disaster strikes, information should reach everyone.
home.disaster_body: Water distribution. Shelters. Supplies. Community updates. Information that matters, in a language you understand.
home.everyday_body: On ordinary days it is the neighbourhood board for building notices, garbage days and local events, so when something happens, people already know where to look.
home.try: To try it, open the board, tap “{button}” and pick one under “{samples}”. The samples are fictional.

about.after_operator: The platform operator creates the boards, connects each city's disaster radio broadcasts to its board once (a mail forwarder, or a reader for the broadcast text the city publishes) and runs the database updates. The operator also keeps the rules every board shares: personal information removed, locations kept coarse, everything deleted when it expires.
about.after_owner: Each board would have a local owner who already puts up the notices: a neighbourhood association (自治会), a building manager, or a desk at the ward office. The owner would hold that board's admin link and use it to confirm official cards, hide what should not be on the board, and switch the board to disaster mode and back.
about.after_new_city: A new city needs data, not new code: its shelters and the districts each one serves, its water points and stations, the district boundaries from the national statistics (e-Stat), and where the city publishes the text of its disaster radio. For the area around one station that is a few hours of work. The checklist is published with the source code (docs/BOARDS.md).
about.after_limits: What is not there yet: today there is one operator, the person who built Engawa, and one admin link opens the admin page of every board. A separate admin link for each board is the next step, so that a local owner can look after their own board without the operator.
